title: Seducing Doctor Lewis
full_review:
A rundown fishing community casts its net in the hopes of catching a miracle in the delightful comedy "Seducing Doctor Lewis" (WellSpring Media).

Making his directorial debut, French-Canadian Jean-Francois Pouliot combines a sweet story with solid across-the-board performances from his ensemble cast to craft a simple but exceptionally well-told tale full of hope and laughter.

In the comedic tradition of "Local Hero" (1983) and "Waking Ned Devine" (1998) -- with shades of TV's "Northern Exposure" -- "Seducing Doctor Lewis" tells the story of a close-knit harbor town on the tiny, impoverished island of Ste.-Marie-La-Mauderne near Montreal. Once a thriving fishing community full of hardworking men who "weren't rich, but were proud," the town has fallen on hard times, forcing its grizzled inhabitants to put down their nets and reluctantly extend their calloused palms for government handouts.

A large Canadian plastics company is considering building a factory on the island, but the investors' proposal comes with one stipulation: The town must, for insurance purposes, prove that it has a full-time resident doctor -- a deal-breaker for the physicianless Ste.-Marie.

Determined not to lose the bid, Ste.-Marie's unofficial leader, Germain (brilliantly played by Raymond Bouchard), rallies the residents to spruce up their ramshackle hamlet and organizes a letter-writing campaign to every doctor in Quebec in the hopes of getting one to take the bait.

Through a series of serendipitous twists a young plastic surgeon from Montreal, the eponymous Dr. Lewis (David Boutin) finds his way to Ste.-Marie. As the title suggests, the bulk of the story revolves around the townspeople trying to "seduce" urban sophisticate Lewis into staying on, by impressing him with Ste.-Marie "big city" amenities.

Of course, how they accomplish this is what makes the film so irresistibly funny. Spearheaded by Germain and his two island cronies -- seaman Yvon (Pierre Collin) and town banker Henri (Benoit Briere) -- the locals, unbeknownst to Lewis, wiretap his telephone in order to find out his likes and dislikes. They then go about customizing the town according to his tastes, putting his favorite dishes on the local pub's menu and fooling him into thinking that they are die-hard cricket fans.

To win him over the hockey-loving islanders even going so far as to stage a hilarious mock cricket match during his arrival on the island. When he flounders at fishing, Yvon scuba-dives under the boat and secretly attaches a frozen fish.

But just when Germain has Lewis hook, line and sinker, the wily old fisherman suffers a pang of conscience over his dishonest ruse, setting up the film's poignant denouement -- an ending which shows that saving lives sometimes entails more than just medicine.

In its home market of French Canada, "Seducing Doctor Lewis" has reeled in more money than either "The Lord of the Rings" or "The Matrix." Much of this is no doubt due to its enchanting fairy tale quality and superb acting, especially the standout performance of Bouchard.

But apart from its captivating artistry, this genial gem celebrates the importance of tradition and ritual in the life of a community.

Through comedy, it also explores the role work plays in enhancing human dignity. Accomplishing it with disarming humor and grace, the film echoes such social encyclicals as "Laborem Exercens" ("On Human Work") in which Pope John Paul II reminds Christians that "work is a good thing" through which man "achieves fulfillment and indeed, in a sense, becomes more of a human being."

As the young Doctor Lewis says of Ste.-Marie, this charming yarn is "small, but extraordinarily true."

Subtitles.

Due to some minor crude language and sexual humor and an instance of drug abuse, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not Rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
